items.en: The Second Dhyāna: Its Name and Cultivation

zh: 次明第二禪者，如偈說：知二法亂心，雖善而應離。如大水澄靜，波蕩亦無見。譬如人大極，安隱睡眠時，若有喚呼聲，其心大惱亂。攝心入禪時，以覺觀為惱，是故除覺觀，得入一識處。內心清淨故，定生得喜樂，得入此二禪，喜勇心大悅。佛以此偈中，廣明中間禪、二禪相。今明二禪有三義：一者、釋名；二、明修行；三、明證相。
en: Next, clarifying the second dhyāna: as the verse says: "Knowing that these two dharmas disturb the mind, though wholesome, they should be left behind. Like a great body of water, still and clear — once waves stir it, nothing can be seen in it. It is like a person, utterly exhausted, resting in peaceful sleep — should a shout suddenly call out, the mind is greatly disturbed and troubled. Gathering the mind to enter dhyāna, initial thought and sustained reflection are themselves felt as a disturbance; hence, removing initial thought and sustained reflection, one is able to enter the abode of a single consciousness. Because the inner mind becomes pure, concentration arises and joy and happiness are attained; entering this second dhyāna, joy leaps up and the mind is greatly delighted." The Buddha, within this verse, clarifies at length the marks of both the intermediate dhyāna and the second dhyāna. Here, the second dhyāna is clarified in three parts: explaining the name; clarifying its cultivation; and clarifying the marks of its realization.

zh: 第一、釋名者，次初禪後，故說二禪。既離覺觀，於第二心得勝支功德，故名二禪，亦名無覺無觀三昧。所以者何？得中間禪，斷覺，二禪內淨發，故斷觀，亦名聖默然定。以覺觀語言滅故，故名默然。若得無漏正慧，入此定故，即名聖默然，《地持論》中說名「喜俱禪」。此定生時，與喜俱發故。
en: First, explaining the name: coming after the first dhyāna, it is thus called the second dhyāna. Having left behind initial thought and sustained reflection, at this second stage of mind one attains a superior factor of merit — hence it is named the second dhyāna, also called the samādhi without initial thought or sustained reflection. Why is this? Upon attaining the intermediate dhyāna, initial thought is cut off; and, as the second dhyāna's own inner purity arises, sustained reflection is cut off as well — hence it is also called the noble concentration of silence, since the path of language through initial thought and sustained reflection has been extinguished, and so it is named "silence." Should one attain uncontaminated right wisdom and enter this concentration, it is then named noble silence. The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise names it "the dhyāna joined with joy," since, when this concentration arises, it arises together with joy.

zh: 第二、修習，即為二：一者、明修習方法；二、明證中間禪。今明修二禪者，若凡夫人，亦當先修六行，佛弟子多修八聖種。聖種義如前說。六行者，謂於初禪第六默然心中厭離覺觀，觀初禪為下苦，知二法動亂，逼惱定心，故為苦。從覺觀生喜樂定等，故為麁。此覺觀法障二禪內淨，故名障。攀上勝者，二禪內淨安隱，勝初禪覺觀動亂之定。妙者，喜定因內淨而發，是為微妙。出者，若得二禪，即心得出離覺觀等障。
en: Second, cultivation: this itself has two parts — clarifying the method of cultivation; and clarifying the realization of the intermediate dhyāna.

Here, clarifying the cultivation of the second dhyāna: an ordinary person should first cultivate the six practices; a disciple of the Buddha, for the most part, cultivates the eight noble lineages instead — the sense of the noble lineages has already been given above. As for the six practices: within the first dhyāna's sixth factor, the mind of silence, one grows weary of and turns away from initial thought and sustained reflection, contemplating the first dhyāna as inferior and as suffering — knowing that these two dharmas disturb and trouble the concentrated mind, and so are suffering; that, arising from initial thought and sustained reflection, joy, happiness, and concentration itself are thereby coarse; that this dharma of initial thought and sustained reflection obstructs the second dhyāna's own inner purity, and so is an obstruction; that reaching for what is superior, the second dhyāna's own inner purity and peace surpasses the first dhyāna's disturbed concentration troubled by initial thought and sustained reflection, and so is excellent; that the joy and concentration born through inner purity is subtle and wondrous; and that, upon attaining the second dhyāna, the mind gains release from the obstruction of initial thought and sustained reflection, and so is an exit.

zh: 復次，行者既知初禪之過障於二禪，今欲遠離，當依三種方便：一、不受不著故得離；二、訶責故得離；三、觀析故得離。譬如世人共事後，見其過失，心欲令去，亦用三法：一者、上人利智不與顏色，前人自去；二者、若不去，應須數責，彼即自去；三者、若不去，當與杖加之，自便去也。若得此三意，可以離初禪覺觀之過。
en: Furthermore: the practitioner, already knowing that the fault of the first dhyāna obstructs the second, and now wishing to leave it far behind, should rely on three expedient means: gaining freedom through neither receiving nor becoming attached to it; gaining freedom through reproach; and gaining freedom through analytic contemplation. It is like people in the world who, having worked together with someone and then seen their faults, wish to see them go — they, too, use three methods: first, a person of superior wisdom simply withholds any warm expression, and the other departs of their own accord; second, if they do not leave, one must reproach them repeatedly, and they will then leave of their own accord; and third, if they still do not leave, one must apply the rod, and they will then be made to leave. If one grasps these same three senses, one is able to leave behind the fault of the first dhyāna's initial thought and sustained reflection.

zh: 二者、明中間禪發相。行者既能深心訶責初禪覺觀，覺觀既滅，五支及默然悉謝。以離初禪，二禪未生，於其中間亦有定法，亦得名禪，但不牢固，無支等扶助之法，所以其心蔑蔑屑屑。然諸師多說為轉寂，心轉初禪默然也。《釋論》說名觀相應，此定以六行觀為體，住此定中。若離六行觀者，則多生憂悔。憂悔心生，則永不發二禪，乃至轉寂亦失，或時還更發初禪，或時合初禪亦失。因是無法自居，到此定時，為山之功而少一簣，當善自慎。經中說為無覺有觀三昧，初禪及默然已謝，但住觀相應心中，修二禪故。
en: Second, clarifying the mark of the intermediate dhyāna's arising: the practitioner, now able to reproach the first dhyāna's initial thought and sustained reflection with a deep and thorough mind, initial thought and sustained reflection thereby extinguished, the five factors and silence both pass away as well. Having left the first dhyāna behind, with the second dhyāna not yet arisen, there is, in the interval between them, a further concentration-dharma present as well, which may also be named dhyāna — though it is not yet secure or firm, without any factor to sustain and support it, and so the mind feels faint and fragmentary. The various masters, for the most part, speak of this as the "shifting stillness," the mind shifting away from the first dhyāna's own silence. The Exegetical Treatise names it "correspondence with contemplation," this concentration taking the contemplation of the six practices as its own substance, abiding within this very concentration.

Should one depart from the contemplation of the six practices, worry and regret arise in abundance instead. Once a mind of worry and regret has arisen, the second dhyāna will never be brought forth at all — and even this very "shifting stillness" will itself be lost; at times, the first dhyāna is instead brought forth once again, and, at other times, even the first dhyāna itself is lost along with it. Left, through this, with no proper footing at all, reaching this concentration and yet falling short of completion for the lack of a single basketful of earth — one must be exceedingly careful here. The sūtra speaks of this as the samādhi without initial thought but with sustained reflection alone: the first dhyāna and its silence having already passed away, one simply abides within the mind that corresponds with contemplation, cultivating the second dhyāna from there.

The three methods for leaving the first dhyāna behind (withholding approval, reproach, force) are the same three-tier escalation already used against demons and against wrong marks in earlier fascicles, now applied to something wholesome rather than harmful — a reminder that even a genuine attainment must eventually be let go of using the same disciplined methods used against outright faults. The intermediate dhyāna's own warning is one of the treatise's more vivid images: reaching this unstable, unsupported halfway state and abandoning the six practices out of worry or impatience is "like a mountain of accomplished work left short for the lack of a single basketful of earth" — the point being that the very last stretch before the second dhyāna is also the most precarious, since neither the first dhyāna's own five factors nor the second dhyāna's own inner purity is yet available to stabilize the mind.

items.en: The Second Dhyāna: Its Arising and Inner Purity
items.zh: 二禪 · 明證相 · 明禪發
parent: The Second Dhyāna: Its Name and Cultivation

zh: 第三、明二禪發相，亦開為六意：一者、明禪發；二、明支義；三、明因果體用；四、明淺深；五、明進退；六、明功德。第一、明二禪發相者，行者於中間禪心不憂悔，一心加功，專精不止，於後其心澹然澄靜，無有分散，名未到地。故論偈云「得入一識處」，即是二禪方便定發。問曰：如論中唯說初禪前有未到地，今二禪前何故復說有未到地？答曰：論總明，故說一。若《舍利弗毘曇》說，有四未到地、四中間禪，今用此義故，更說有未到地及中間也。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of the second dhyāna's own arising: this, too, opens into six parts — clarifying dhyāna's own arising; clarifying the meaning of its factors; clarifying its cause, effect, substance, and function; clarifying its depth; clarifying its progress and regression; and clarifying its merits.

First, clarifying the mark of the second dhyāna's own arising: the practitioner, within the intermediate dhyāna, the mind free of worry and regret, applies effort single-mindedly, devoted and unceasing; afterward, the mind grows calm and clear, without any scattering at all — this is named the "not-yet-arrived" state. Hence the treatise verse says, "one is able to enter the abode of a single consciousness" — this is precisely the arising of the second dhyāna's own preliminary concentration.

Question: the treatise speaks of a "not-yet-arrived" state only before the first dhyāna — why, then, is a "not-yet-arrived" state now spoken of before the second dhyāna as well? Answer: the treatise speaks in general terms, and so speaks of only a single such state. The Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra, however, speaks of four "not-yet-arrived" states and four intermediate dhyānas — here, following this same sense, a "not-yet-arrived" state and an intermediate state are spoken of here as well.

zh: 經久不失不退，專心不止，於後其心豁然明淨皎潔，定心與喜俱發。亦如人從暗室中出，見外日月光明，其心豁然明亮。內淨十種功德眷屬俱發之義，具如初禪發相，但以從內淨定俱發為異耳。復次，二禪喜樂等發，不從外來，一心澄淨大喜，美妙清淨，勝初禪故，論云：「內心清淨故，定生得喜樂，得入此二禪，喜勇心大悅。」
en: Once this state has persisted for a long while without loss or regression, the mind applied single-mindedly and without ceasing, afterward the mind opens out, bright, pure, and radiant, the concentrated mind arising together with joy — just like a person emerging from a darkened room and seeing the sun and moon's own outer light, the mind opening out, bright and clear. The sense of the ten kinds of merit arising together as its retinue, through this very inner purity, is exactly as already given for the first dhyāna's own arising — differing only in that here they arise together through inner-purity concentration specifically. Furthermore, the second dhyāna's joy and happiness arise not from anything external at all, but from a single mind of pure clarity and great joy, wondrous and pure, surpassing the first dhyāna — hence the treatise says: "Because the inner mind becomes pure, concentration arises and joy and happiness are attained; entering this second dhyāna, joy leaps up and the mind is greatly delighted."

zh: 云何名為內淨？遠而言之，對外塵故，說內淨；近而言之，對內垢故，說內淨。所以者何？如初禪中得觸樂時，身即明淨，兼令心淨。觸是身識相應，故名外淨。今待初禪外淨，故說二禪心識相應為內淨，亦令身淨，淨身故，名外淨。內淨是心淨，淨從心出，令身亦淨，故言內淨。今言待內垢，故說內淨者，初禪之中，心為覺觀所動，故名為內垢。今得二禪，內心無有覺觀之垢，故名為內淨。
en: What is meant by "inner purity"? Discussed broadly, it is spoken of in contrast to external sense-objects; discussed narrowly, it is spoken of in contrast to inward defilement. Why is this? Just as, within the first dhyāna, when tactile happiness is attained, the body itself becomes bright and pure, and this, in turn, causes the mind to become pure as well — since tactile sensation corresponds to body-consciousness, this is named outer purity. Here, in relation to the first dhyāna's own outer purity, the second dhyāna's correspondence with mind-consciousness is said to be inner purity — and this, in turn, also causes the body to become pure; because the body is thereby purified, this is named outer purity in its own right. Inner purity is purity of mind — purity issuing from the mind causes the body, too, to become pure — hence it is called "inner" purity. As for saying it is spoken of in contrast to inward defilement: within the first dhyāna, the mind is stirred by initial thought and sustained reflection, and so this is named inward defilement; now, having attained the second dhyāna, the inner mind is free of the defilement of initial thought and sustained reflection, and so is named inner purity.

zh: 言定生得喜樂者，上於初禪說離生，今此說定生，義意云何？正言初禪離欲界，生色界定法故，二禪既無此義，但說定生。問曰：若爾，虛空定亦應說離生邪？答曰：不然。前已受名，故不應重說。又且虛空離色界，但發定之時而無支林等法生，故不說離生。問曰：初禪亦有喜樂，與此何異？答曰：彼從覺觀生喜樂，與身識相應。此中喜樂從內心生，還與意識相應，以此為異。
en: As for the phrase "concentration arises, and joy and happiness are attained": above, in the case of the first dhyāna, "born of separation" was spoken of; here, "concentration arises" is spoken of instead — what is the sense of this difference? Properly speaking, the first dhyāna is spoken of as "born of separation" because it separates from the desire realm and gives birth to the dharma of form-realm concentration; the second dhyāna, having no such sense, is instead spoken of simply as "concentration arising."

Question: if this is so, should the concentration of boundless space not likewise be spoken of as "born of separation"? Answer: this does not follow. The name has already been given once before, and so should not be spoken of again in the same way; and, further, the concentration of boundless space, though it leaves the form realm behind, has no grove-of-factors dharma arising at the moment concentration is brought forth, and so is not spoken of as "born of separation" either.

Question: the first dhyāna, too, has joy and happiness — how does this differ from the second dhyāna's own? Answer: there, joy and happiness arise from initial thought and sustained reflection, and correspond with body-consciousness. Here, joy and happiness arise from the inner mind itself, and correspond instead with mind-consciousness — this is how they differ.

"Inner purity" gets the same double-angle treatment "factor" received in the first dhyāna — broad sense (versus external objects) and narrow sense (versus the internal defilement of initial thought and sustained reflection), plus a further inner/outer distinction where the second dhyāna's own "inner" purity of mind causes a secondary "outer" purity of body, mirroring but surpassing the first dhyāna's purity, which ran the other direction (body to mind). The precise vocabulary distinction between "born of separation" (reserved for the first dhyāna, which separates from the desire realm and gives birth to form-realm concentration) and "concentration arising" (used for the second dhyāna, which has no such separation) is sharpened by the follow-up question: even the sphere of boundless space, which does leave the form realm behind, is not called "born of separation," because no grove of factors arises when its concentration is brought forth. This is a good example of how carefully this treatise tracks its own terminology — a difference in wording here is never incidental, always cashing out to a specific doctrinal point when questioned.

quiz.q: What else is the second dhyāna called?
options: the samādhi without initial thought or reflection, the concentration of noble silence, the dhyāna joined with joy
quiz.why: "Also called the samādhi without initial thought or sustained reflection ... also called the noble concentration of silence ... The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise names it 'the dhyāna joined with joy,' since, when this concentration arises, it arises together with joy."

quiz.q: Under what condition is it called "noble silence"?
options: with thought and language extinguished it is "silence"; entering it with uncontaminated right wisdom makes it "noble silence"
quiz.why: "Since the path of language through initial thought and sustained reflection has been extinguished, and so it is named 'silence.' Should one attain uncontaminated right wisdom and enter this concentration, it is then named noble silence."

quiz.q: In cultivating the second dhyāna, what do ordinary people and disciples practice, and where are the six practices cultivated?
options: ordinary people the six practices, disciples mostly the eight noble lineages; within the first dhyāna's sixth, silent mind, turning away from thought and reflection
quiz.why: "An ordinary person should first cultivate the six practices; a disciple of the Buddha, for the most part, cultivates the eight noble lineages instead ... As for the six practices: within the first dhyāna's sixth factor ... one grows weary of and turns away from initial thought and sustained reflection."

quiz.q: What simile illustrates the three expedient means for leaving the first dhyāna's thought and reflection?
options: like wishing someone gone: withhold warmth and they leave; if not, reproach them; if still not, apply the rod
quiz.why: "Gaining freedom through neither receiving nor becoming attached to it; gaining freedom through reproach; and gaining freedom through analytic contemplation. It is like people in the world who, having worked together with someone and then seen their faults, wish to see them go — they, too, use three methods."

quiz.q: What is the intermediate dhyāna like, and what do the masters and the Exegetical Treatise call it?
options: between the first and second, a concentration not yet firm, the mind faint; the masters call it "shifting stillness," the treatise "correspondence with contemplation"
quiz.why: "Having left the first dhyāna behind, with the second dhyāna not yet arisen, there is, in the interval between them, a further concentration-dharma present as well ... though it is not yet secure or firm ... The various masters, for the most part, speak of this as the 'shifting stillness' ... The Exegetical Treatise names it 'correspondence with contemplation.'"

quiz.q: If one departs from the six-practice contemplation while in the intermediate dhyāna, what happens, and what image warns of it?
options: worry and regret arise; the second never comes, the shifting stillness is lost, even the first may be lost — like a mountain short of one basket of earth
quiz.why: "Should one depart from the contemplation of the six practices, worry and regret arise in abundance instead. Once a mind of worry and regret has arisen, the second dhyāna will never be brought forth at all ... reaching this concentration and yet falling short of completion for the lack of a single basketful of earth."

quiz.q: What samādhi does the sūtra call the intermediate dhyāna?
options: the samādhi without initial thought but with sustained reflection
quiz.why: "The sūtra speaks of this as the samādhi without initial thought but with sustained reflection alone: the first dhyāna and its noble silence having already passed away, one simply abides within the mind that corresponds with contemplation."

quiz.q: The treatise speaks of a not-yet-arrived state only before the first dhyāna. Why is one spoken of before the second?
options: the treatise speaks generally of one; the Śāriputra-abhidharma speaks of four not-yet-arrived states and four intermediate dhyānas
quiz.why: "The treatise speaks in general terms, and so speaks of only a single such state. The Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra, however, speaks of four 'not-yet-arrived' states and four intermediate dhyānas."

quiz.q: When the second dhyāna's concentration arises with joy, what simile is used?
options: like emerging from a dark room and seeing the sun and moon, the mind opening bright and clear
quiz.why: "Afterward the mind opens out, bright, pure, and radiant, the concentrated mind arising together with joy — just like a person emerging from a darkened room and seeing the sun and moon's own outer light."

quiz.q: What two explanations of "inner purity" does the text give?
options: broadly, contrasted with outer objects (first-dhyāna touch is body-consciousness, outer; the second corresponds to mind-consciousness, inner); narrowly, contrasted with inner defilement (thought and reflection)
quiz.why: "Discussed broadly, it is spoken of in contrast to external sense-objects; discussed narrowly, it is spoken of in contrast to inward defilement ... within the first dhyāna, the mind is stirred by initial thought and sustained reflection, and so this is named inward defilement."

quiz.q: How do the joy and happiness of the first dhyāna differ from those of the second?
options: the first's arise from thought and reflection with body-consciousness; the second's from the inner mind with mind-consciousness
quiz.why: "There, joy and happiness arise from initial thought and sustained reflection, and correspond with body-consciousness. Here, joy and happiness arise from the inner mind itself, and correspond instead with mind-consciousness — this is how they differ."

quiz.q: Since the concentration of boundless space also leaves the form realm, why is it not called "born of leaving"?
options: the name was already given before; and no grove of factors arises when it arises
it does not leave the form realm
quiz.why: "The name has already been given once before, and so should not be spoken of again in the same way; and, further, the concentration of boundless space, though it leaves the form realm behind, has no grove-of-factors dharma arising at the moment concentration is brought forth."
